TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
MONDAY, 10 AUGUST 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 8, DAY 4
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
RICHARD LANCASTER SC WITH ZELIE HEGER SC, TAMARA
PHILLIPS AND ALISON HAMMOND, COUNSEL ASSISTING

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Phillips.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I call Susan Woodward AM.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Woodward, will you take an oath or make an affirmation.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: An affirmation, thank you, Commissioner.
<SUSAN WOODWARD, AFFIRMED
COMMISSIONER: Do take a seat.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Thank you.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you please state your full name.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Susan Dorothy Woodward.
MS PHILLIPS: You are the Commissioner of Australian Charities and Not-for-profits
Commission.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, I am.
MS PHILLIPS: You have prepared a witness statement dated 29 July 2026?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have included a table within that statement at paragraph 61, and
since preparing your statement, is it right that you have identified some corrections to that
table which have been included in a separate document?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct, the formatting had gone astray.
MS PHILLIPS: And if one replaces the table in your witness statement with that separate
document that you provided, is the statement true and correct to the best of your
knowledge and belief?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, it is.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I tender the witness statement and the accompanying
table. They have document IDs STA.0557.0001.0001 for the statement, and the table is
ACN.7999.0001.0012.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, the two documents will be received as exhibits.

MS PHILLIPS: You were appointed to the position as full-time Commissioner of the
Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission, which I might refer to as the ACNC,
for a five-year term in December 2022; is that right?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And prior to your appointment, you'd held senior leadership roles in
Justice Connect, a legal assistance charity, and you'd also worked for a long time in various
other roles in the not-for-profit sector?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: You have academic qualifications in law; is that right?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have taught over many years in the areas of corporations law,
corporate governance, not-for-profit organisations, both as a lecturer and then as a senior
fellow at the University of Melbourne?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's right.
MS PHILLIPS: The ACNC was established and began operating in December of 2012;
is that right?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, it is.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have described it in your witness statement as a relatively new
agency.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: In regulated terms, it's still considered fairly
new. Possibly we are getting to our teenage years, but certainly we are not as well
established as some.
MS PHILLIPS: And your role as Commissioner of the ACNC, that's a statutory office
that is established pursuant to the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
Act?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: The statutory objects of that legislation are set out in the Act and you
have extracted these at paragraph 7 of your witness statement. One of those objects is:
"To maintain, protect and enhance public trust and confidence in the Australian
not-for-profit sector."
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's accurate.

MS PHILLIPS: And another is:
"To support and sustain a robust, vibrant, independent and innovative Australia
not-for-profit sector."
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And another is to promote the reduction of unnecessary regulatory
obligations this that sector?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it the case that the ACNC was formed after a Productivity
Commission report had identified a need for regulatory reform to improve accountability,
transparency and public confidence within the not-for-profit sector?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that was one of many reports. That was
the most pivotal one, I think, in spurring the establishment of the ACNC.
MS PHILLIPS: And one of the reform proposals I think you've referred to in paragraph 9
in your witness statement of that Productivity Commission report had been that the
Australian Government establish a national regulator for the sector with responsibility for
determining charitable status, maintaining a public register, providing sector guidance and
undertaking regulatory oversight; is that right?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Is it your understanding that the ACNC was established broadly to give
effect to those recommendations?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, it is.
MS PHILLIPS: A key statutory function of the Commissioner of the ACNC from time to
time is to register eligible not-for-profit entities of certain types or subtypes of charity; is
that correct?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, it is. It is a voluntary registration process.
MS PHILLIPS: And in your statement, you have noted that when we talk about Not-for-
profits, it doesn't necessarily mean that the entity in question can't or won't make a profit.
Can you explain that?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. It can be confusing. All charities must
operate on a not-for-profit basis but not all not-for-profit organisations are eligible to be
registered as a charity, and the confusing thing happens with the words "not-for-profit".
A charity can't operate while it is insolvent; that is not allowed. But it's what happens with

the profits that really distinguishes between a charity and, if you like, a business. So the
profits, the revenue raised from the organisation, have to be used for the charitable
purpose.
MS PHILLIPS: And in terms of an entity that is a not-for-profit but that might not be
eligible to be registered as a charity, I think you have given in your witness statement the
example of a community sporting club. And is the reason that that kind of not-for-profit
entity won't be able to be registered as a charity because its purpose isn't a charitable
purpose of the kind recognised in the charities legislation?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Now, where entities do meet the legal definition of a charity under the
Charities Act, how does registration as a charity with the ACNC affect their ability,
typically, to access Commonwealth tax concessions?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: As I said, it is a voluntary system. So you
don't have to register. But the incentive to register includes that you must be a registered
charity if you want to access Commonwealth taxation and other concessional benefits. So
it is a pathway, a requirement, a stepping stone, if you like, to that.
MS PHILLIPS: And in your witness statement - this is at paragraph 46 - you have
identified that some of those concessions might include an income tax exemption, GST
concessions, fringe benefits tax rebates and, for some charities, a fringe benefits tax
exemption as well?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that the particular tax concessions that are available to
charities that are registered with the ACNC something which can depend on the type of
charity that an entity is registered as?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. That's right. There are certain subtypes
that when the - so the tax concessions are administered by the ATO, the Australian
Taxation Office, and they'll look at which particular subtype the charity has been registered
for, because that will affect what they're eligible for in terms of concessions.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've described at paragraph 47 of your witness statement DGR,
or ‘deductible gift recipient’ endorsement, as a highly sought-after form of tax concession.
Is it your understanding that when an entity is endorsed by the ATO as a deductible gift
recipient, donors to the charity can receive a tax deduction for the donations that they
make?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've identified that DGR endorsement is something that is
administered by the ATO and not by the ACNC; is that right?

COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's right.
MS PHILLIPS: How do you understand the ACNC's registration of an entity as
a particular charitable type or subtype to feed in, as it were, to the ATO's process of
endorsement of DGRs?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: There are some categories, some subtypes that
we would register a charity for that then, in a way, effectively mean that they are
almost - you know, subject to the ATO doing their processes, will give them that pathway.
The most common one in relation to deductible gift recipient, DGR, status would be a term
that is called public benevolent institution. So if - we determine that part. So we look at
the particulars of the registration application and the activities and purposes. And if they
meet that category, that can smooth the path to - the Tax Office will accept that and then
they'll apply their taxation provisions to that.
MS PHILLIPS: So your understanding in the case of public benevolent institutions, for
example, is if the ACNC has registered an entity with that charity subtype or type, as
a matter of course, ordinarily, DGR endorsement by the ATO would follow?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And in terms of the broader delineation of functions between yourself as
the ACNC Commissioner and the Commissioner of Taxation, or the Australian Tax Office,
at a broad level, is it right that the function of the ACNC Commissioner is to determine
first whether an entity should be registered as a particular type of charity and then possibly
over time to consider enforcement mechanisms and whether the entity is entitled to retain
that registration?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, it is. When you are a registered charity,
you also have obligations to provide annual information. So that's a way that may
also - that information typically appears on the public register and that can also support the
work conducted by the Australian Taxation Office.
MS PHILLIPS: And, broadly, when it comes to charities, is it right that the role of the
Commissioner of Taxation is to administer the taxation laws to entities based upon their
charitable registration status as it has been determined by the ACNC Commissioner?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: At paragraph 11 of your witness statement, you have given some figures
of the rise in the total number of charities in Australia over the decade from 30 June 2015
to 30 June 2025. Can I ask you to comment on that trend as you've identified it?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. The number did - when the ACNC was
first established, the number varied a little bit because it was establishing a new register
and, you know, there was some that had - needed to come off and some that came on. And

then for a period of time, it was relatively stable at around 60,000. The number in the last
few years has risen to over 66,000 charities, primarily because of a new reporting
provision that the ATO are administering. So if an organisation wants to be income tax
exempt, they may - if they want to be income tax exempt, unless they're a registered
charity, they will have to now report separately to the ATO. And this has meant a lot of
organisations that perhaps falsely thought they were entitled to operate as a not-for-profit
and didn't need to register as a charity have now realised they do need to register with us,
otherwise they run the risk of having to pay income tax on any net income that they make.
So it has brought forward an increase in the total number of registered charities.
MS PHILLIPS: And I think you have given a figure of about 17 per cent in terms of total
number of charities as between 2015 to 2025; does that sound correct?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. Over that decade, when you look back at
the figures, it is about a 17 per cent increase.
MS PHILLIPS: And I think you have identified in your statement that in the 2024 to
2025 year, perhaps on account of the measures that you have just been describing, there
was the highest number of new charity registrations in a single year since ACNC was
established?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, that's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Has there been a commensurate increase, to your understanding, in the
budget allocation to the ACNC's operations over time to reflect, perhaps, the growth in the
total number of charities that are registered with the agency?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That increase is in the last few years. There
hasn't been a particular allocation to reflect that. We did receive support from the
Australian Taxation Commissioner by way of extra staff to deal with that flow-on. So
under the ACNC Act, the ATO Commissioner makes staff available to me as the ACNC
Commissioner. I direct the staff and have that independence. Recognising there was this
flow-on effect, the Tax Commissioner did make some additional staff available to us to
support us with some of that workload.
MS PHILLIPS: At paragraph 14 of your statement, you have identified the significant
role that charities play within Australia's economy, community life and workforce. And
you've given a figure that a report in relation - that was published on 11 June 2026,
identified the generation of $239 billion in revenue. First of all, is that in relation to the
2024 reporting period, so an annual - on an annual basis?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. So what happens is that registered
charities need to report to us annually. We call it an annual information statement. And as
part of the commitment when the ACNC was established, that - we have taken very
seriously the responsibility to report back, you know, the accumulation of that data to
better inform the public about the sector, and to show, really, the incredible economic

significance that the sector has. So that is data from the 2024 reporting period and, as you
say, it does identify that amount of money in terms of total revenue.
MS PHILLIPS: And over at paragraph 17 of your statement, you have identified the
proportion of that $239 billion that's come from government, and can I ask you to
comment on that?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. The sector gets its income from a range
of sources, and when you look up our register, Commissioner, for any particular charity, it
does show where, for any particular charity, the high level of where their revenue comes
from, whether it's from government grants - and that could be grants from local
government, state government or federal - or whether it's from donations and bequests, or
whether it's income they have generated themselves.
And collating that all together, it shows overall that nearly, about 48 per cent of the total
income for the entire sector - registered charities sector is from government sources. I
think it is, just if you indulge me, important to note, though, that that's not every single
charity gets government funding. In fact, the vast majority are small and would not get
government funding. But the government is a major contributor, often by contracting
charities to provide important services.
MS PHILLIPS: And that figure of 118 billion, which is about the just less than half of
the 239 that you have identified in your statement, is that just government income? Would
that factor in, for example, the value of deductions that donors might receive from making
donations to DGRs?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: No, that is actual government income,
typically by way of contract - government contracts, or government grants. And it's not
just federal government; it would also be the other layers of government.
MS PHILLIPS: And can I take you to paragraph 18 of your statement. You've noted
there that charities occupy a position of substantial public trust, and you've also drawn
attention to the public contributions that are made to charities. How do you see those
aspects affecting the sort of governance and regulation that are required in the charity
sector?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: As you outlined before, a key one of our
statutory objects, which is in some respects a North Star, a guiding principle for the way
that we operate, is around a role in ensuring public trust and confidence in this sector,
particularly because the sector is such a vital sector that relies on public trust in terms of
public - the public donating, in terms of the public volunteering, and also in terms of the
government contribution and the funding contribution to the sector. I think it's right that
we recognise that the sector is both an economic and social significance, and with that
comes, if you like, a corresponding responsibility to honour and comply with basic
principles to ensure ongoing public trust and confidence in that sector.

MS PHILLIPS: I'd like to ask you next about some of the more granular mechanics of
how the ACNC Act operates, perhaps starting out by introducing some of the key terms
that you have gone through in your witness statement, as well as the constitutional footing
of the ACNC Act itself. First of all, at paragraphs 50 and 51 of your statement, you have
explained that the ACNC Act uses the term "responsible entity". Can you outline at a high
level who a responsible entity is and what that refers to?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: I'm afraid, Commissioner, the Act is not
written in a very user-friendly way but obviously technically correct. So we have the term
in the Act "responsible entity", and I think if you think of that, that's the charity, the
registered charity. It also talks about - so, sorry, there's "registered entity", which is the
charity, and then there is "responsible entities" or "responsible people". I would
summarise that down to the charity, the registered charity, or the people governing the
organisation that are actually on our register as being what we call "responsible people", so
the people that have been nominated by that charity essentially governing the charity, so,
you know, the board of directors, the committee of management for an incorporated
association.
MS PHILLIPS: And I will come back to this a bit later, but I will just note that at
paragraph 52 of your statement you have identified that the ACNC or the ACNC
Commissioner, has limited powers in relation to responsible entities particularly in the
circumstances set out in division 100 of the Act, but I will bring you back to that.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, okay. Thank you.
MS PHILLIPS: Then at paragraph 54, you have outlined that the ACNC Act, in terms of
its enactment originally principally relied on particular Commonwealth constitutional
powers, including the corporations power, and also the territories power. In a broad sense,
are you able to outline the implications of that constitutional footing, particularly for the
ability of the ACNC Commissioner to be given powers to regulate responsible persons?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. The residual powers rest with the states
and territories, the states for charities. And so my understanding - and I'm not
a constitutional lawyer and it's not my job to do that, but at a broad level, the ACNC Act
draws on that corporations power that the Commonwealth has. The territories power,
when it comes to our external conduct standards, rely on that power and also for other
provisions, the taxation power becomes relevant. So the foundation of why it's a voluntary
system is that people will be voluntarily registering, then the taxation powers are enlivened
because they are registering so they can access those taxation benefits. So that's the
grounding for the ACNC Act, noting that the state attorneys will keep residual powers over
charitable trusts and assets, for example.
MS PHILLIPS: The next concept that you've introduced in your witness statement is one
called a ‘federally regulated entity’, or an FRE, to use the acronym. In broad terms, are
these entities corporations that the Australian constitution permits to be regulated under
Commonwealth legislation as constitutional corporations, as it were?

COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, sometimes it again can get a little bit
technical and confusing. It is - there's a range of things that have to be considered in order
to meet the definition in the Act - or there's no actual definition in the Act about what is
a federally regulated entity but it draws on that constitutional law concept. It's not a simple
that if a charity, registered charity, is a corporation under the Corporations Act that it meets
this test. So it's more about whether it's a trading entity, and a whole range of other
factors. So it is quite a technical area.
MS PHILLIPS: And are you able to give a high-level example of a charity or a charity
structure that might be registered as a charity with the ACNC but which would not be
a federally regulated entity?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Perhaps an example would be - let's take
a child care centre. If it was a child care centre in the ACT, that is a territory. That would
enliven - that is one example where it meets the federally regulated entity test very clearly.
Another child care centre just across the border in New South Wales is probably not going
to meet that test because they probably don't meet the bar of, you know, trading, in trading
commerce, for example.
MS PHILLIPS: And of the I think 66-odd thousand registered charities that I think you
gave the figure for before, does the ACNC have oversight at any given time as to how
many of them meet that definition of an FRE or a federally regulated entity?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: No, we don't. We can't know at any point in
time how many of the 66,000 are federally regulated entities,, primarily because it is
a point in time assessment and it can change, and, as I say, it's not a clear-cut line that
entirely links to their legal structure.
MS PHILLIPS: And the next term that you have addressed at paragraph 58 of your
witness statement is a ‘basic religious charity’ or a BRC. And you've outlined the criteria
for that kind of entity there. Can you give an overview of what the criteria are for an invite
to be classed as a basic religious charity?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, they're set out in full in the statement at
paragraph 58. There are six criteria, and, primarily, they must be entirely for the subtype
of advancing religion. So they can't have an additional subtype, for example, advancing
education. They must not be a body corporate. So if they're an incorporated association or
a company or incorporated under other legislation, then that will mean they can't meet the
test. Except with limited exceptions, they can't have that deductible gift recipient status
that we talked about before. They can't be part of a reporting group, which has a particular
meaning.
There's also a monetary limit. If they receive grant funding from an Australian
Government agency, there's a limit of 100,000 over two financial years. So, you know, if
they receive quite significant government grant funding, they won't be eligible. The last
requirement is that they - if they are required to participate in the National Redress Scheme

for Institutional Child Sexual Abuse and they've been identified as an entity relevant for
that, they can't be - they can't remain as a basic religious charity.
MS PHILLIPS: I'd like to ask you next about the processes for registering and the criteria
for registering a charity of the various kinds. At paragraph 24 of your statement, you've
extracted the various criteria that an entity needs to meet in order to be registered as
a charity. So is it right that amongst those are that the charity needs to be a not-for-profit
and to have an ABN as well?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Sorry, is it paragraph 24?
MS PHILLIPS: Sorry, I might have directed you to the wrong - I think 74.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's all right. Sorry, which one did you say?
I know it's there, but -
MS PHILLIPS: It's 74 on page 19.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Okay, thank you.
MS PHILLIPS: Sorry about that.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Then, sorry, what was the question?
MS PHILLIPS: Is it right that you have extracted at this part of your statement the
conditions that an entity needs to meet in order to be registered by the ACNC as a charity?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, I have. Thank you.
MS PHILLIPS: And they include the entity is a not-for-profit entity and that it has an
Australian Business Number?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have also identified that one of the conditions for registration is
that the entity is in compliance with the Governance Standards and the External Conduct
Standards?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes. Just to maybe add a further clarification,
in terms of the Governance Standards, basic religious charities do not have to apply with
the Governance Standards. So that's not applicable to them.
MS PHILLIPS: So that won't be a registration criterion for those charities, compliance
with those standards?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes.

MS PHILLIPS: And the standards themselves, they are set out in the ACNC's regulations
later in the Act?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have extracted a summary of the Governance Standards as
appearing in the regulations at paragraph 77 of your witness statement. Can I just take up
a couple of them with you. Is it right that Governance Standard 3, which you have referred
to at 77.3 of your statement, that requires that charities not act in a way that would, under
Commonwealth, state or territory law, could be dealt with as an indictable offence or
a breach of a law that has a civil penalty, carrying 60 penalty units or more?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And so that's a standard that applies to charitable entities or applicants to
become charitable entities themselves, not to the representatives or the responsible persons
of those entities?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, our entire framework is capped very
much on - our powers are over the entity, not over the individual people governing that
organisation.
MS PHILLIPS: And, in practice, at the point of registration of an entity or seeking to be
registered as a charity, how would the ACNC go about trying to work out whether
a charity has committed, say, an indictable offence such as to fall foul of Governance
Standard 3?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: We do cause searches. So we would look at,
for example, whether anyone named in the application was associated with - was
disqualified on the ASIC register, if anyone was on a sanctioned list like the DFAT
sanctioned list. We do other - you know, there's top searches. Primarily, I just perhaps
highlight the context that usually when we're considering an application, if it's a new
entity, it can be quite difficult because, of course, they're saying, "This is what we are
going to do. This is our proposed constitution. These are the proposed people." They
haven't actually already, you know, done activities in the name of the entity itself. So we
also have a risk framework. So if we feel that it's - it comes up on our risk framework that
we have some reason to be more concerned, we would do more detailed searching.
MS PHILLIPS: Just as a hypothetical, whether it's at the pre-registration or the
post-registration stage, if you had a circumstance where it was known or it became known
that a director of a charitable entity had committed an indictable offence, is it right that that
wouldn't necessarily cause the charity itself to contravene Governance Standard 3? Is that
your understanding?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct. Governance Standard 3 talks
about the entity. So the charity must not commit the offence. Some of those indictable
offences will apply to an entity, but often it might apply to an individual. So under that

Governance Standard, it's not a sort of given that that breach flows through to the charity's
breach.
MS PHILLIPS: And one might need to look at principles of corporate attribution in
terms of corporate governance law and the like to work out the circumstances in which an
offence by a director, say, can be attributed to the corporate entity itself?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct. Was that person authorised by the
charity to make that statement, do that activity? Or was it, you know, a volunteer
associated with the entity that was doing it, perhaps, as a bit of a rogue or isolated event.
MS PHILLIPS: Can I take you to paragraph 77.4 of your statement, where you have
referred to Governance Standard 4. You have said there that under this standard:
"Charities must take reasonable steps to ensure that their responsible persons are suitable
to hold those positions and are not disqualified from managing a corporation or barred by
the ACNC."
Can I just check with you, does the regulation that gives effect to Governance Standard 4
at the moment include any broad test of suitability for responsible persons of charities?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: No, it doesn't. It's just simply the two matters
that you mentioned.
MS PHILLIPS: And so is it the case that, to your understanding currently under the
regulation giving effect to Governance Standard 4, the reasonable steps that charities must
take are limited to ensuring that responsible persons first aren't disqualified from managing
a corporation, and second, have not been disqualified previously by the ACNC itself?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's the minimum standard that they would
need to satisfy. When we work with charities, we often see that they might have broader
requirements for screening their directors, but that's what's required under that Governance
Standard yes.
MS PHILLIPS: But by the ACNC legislation itself?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And then Governance Standard 5, is that broadly about the need for an
entity to ensure that their responsible persons undertake proper management of the
charitable organisation?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, I think this standard can sometimes
confuse people, because it has a sub-list of all the - what you would probably describe as
fairly typical director-type duties. But the Governance Standard is again on the charity as
an entity, and that goes back to that constitutional limitation you raised earlier. So it's
a standard that talks about the charity must take reasonable steps to ensure that its

responsible people, its directors, understand and comply with then the list of duties under
underneath that.
MS PHILLIPS: You mentioned Governance Standard 6 earlier, which deals with
obligations of entities identified as having been involved in institutional child sex abuse.
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: And who should be - are members of the
National Redress Scheme, correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Another registration you have identified is compliance with External
Conduct Standards, and you've extracted or summarised these at paragraph 78 of your
statement. Is it right that those External Conduct Standards apply to all charities, including
basic religious charities?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: That's correct. To enliven the External
Conduct Standards, a charity, including a basic religious charity, must - would be
conducting activities or sending funds overseas.
MS PHILLIPS: And, broadly, is it the case that those External Conduct Standards relate
to activities that take place outside of Australia or that have some connection with
activities outside of Australia?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: Yes, exactly.
MS PHILLIPS: Another condition for registration of a charity is the one that you've
referred to at paragraph 74.4 of your witness statement, that an:
"...entity is not covered by a decision in writing made by an Australian government agency
(including a judicial officer) under an Australian law that provides for entities for
characterised on the basis of them engaging in, or supporting, is terrorist or other
criminal activities."
What steps does the ACNC take to try and identify the existence of any such decision and
what form might such decisions take?
COMMISSIONER WOODWARD AM: We would also check the sanctioned list. So
the sanction lists - I think it's by DFAT - about whether either the entity itself is sanctioned
or any individual that might be connected with, in the case of a registration application, the

which I didn't feel was appropriate as a first step to introduce the young person or his
family to a police program.
MS HAMMOND: And when you indicated that you weren't seeking direction to a police
intervention program, what then happened in your conversation with the representative on
the hotline?
ADE: This is when I called the national help line, pretty much they weren't able to direct
me to anything, and just gave me general advice of other counselling types of services and
tips which were available on the website. And, you know, I stated that, you know, I could
find a general counsellor myself and I don't think that was going to be helpful in the
situation, because with young people and with this young person, I think they've had - a lot
of people have already had enough exposure to counsellors and other people that don't get
them. So being exposed to another person who didn't understand or didn't get them,
I didn't think it was going to be helpful.
MS HAMMOND: What had you hoped the National Support Hotline might have been
able to provide you with?
ADE: Yes, I had hoped to access, like, independence specialist support from a counsellor
or psychologist in our city that was not connected to a police program; practical education
materials, especially for the family; clear information about the size and progression of
radicalisation; and, in particular, the groups that are influencing young people and the
broader community - because that wasn't on the website at all about who actually is in the
community.

MS HAMMOND: And it sounds like you spent some time on the Step Together website;
is that right?
ADE: Yes, I tried to.
MS HAMMOND: Can you explain to the Commission your general impression of the
Step Together website?
ADE: Sure. Well, firstly, no disrespect to anyone who built it, I found the website poorly
designed and difficult to navigate, and I'd imagine someone who is not familiar with
getting around a website or with a topic would find it a challenge. Much of the
information on the website was vague or general or you really had to kind of dig,
dig - click many links to find it. And some of the links didn't work, or went places that
weren't helpful.
While the available - and at the end of the day, the available support program is a police
intervention program. There was little or no information about the specific groups or
patterns of behaviour, including those associated with far-right extremism or neo-Nazi
beliefs, which I found troubling. I also found that the website could be difficult for
someone unfamiliar, as I said, with radicalisation.
To help educate my young relative's family and myself about the Australian and
international groups from which he had been obtaining information, or with which he may
have been involved, I really had to independently research myself and compile lists of
various resources, you know, like news articles and videos and various documentaries. It
was also something a little bit troubling with the website that, on the front page, it kind
of - it states something which appears to separate radicalisation from violent extremism,
stating that:
"Radicalisation is only wanting drastic change in society. It doesn't mean that person is
going to be violent."
You know, like, that it's okay to have, you know, radical thoughts of a drastic change in
society - which I do agree with - but in doing so, it really risks misrepresenting the very
real social and personal harms caused by far-right radicalisation and overlooks that
spectrum between physical and non-physical violence. So it felt like, you know, your child
could be acting out in all manners of way but if they're not blowing something up or
somebody up, you know, this website is not for you.
So where do we go between something doesn't feel right - and I do want to say that when
I say I don't want this young person to cause anyone harm, I'm talking verbal harm as well.
I'm talking about excluding people. I'm talking about the serious harm that comes from the
expression of some of these ideologies. That, to me, is equally as harmful as violent
extremism.

MS HAMMOND: One of the things you mention in your statement is that when you
engaged with Step Together and spoke to the person, having called the hotline, you had
some uncertainties about confidentiality?
ADE: Sure, yes.
MS HAMMOND: Can you speak to that a little bit?
ADE: Yes, it wasn't until after the call that I went, oh gosh, they didn't - I don't recall any
confidentiality statement being read out to me. And then I was surprised a few days later,
somebody called me back from the town that I live in. I recently called the hotline again
just to check it out, and what came up this time was an automated recording at the
beginning of the call stating that the call would be recorded. I did hang up at that point.
And had I received that notification when I first called, I would have hung up as well. I
believe others may respond similarly, particularly if they're concerned that information
disclosed during the call could incriminate themselves or someone else.
So I don't think that's helpful, that you are being told even before you speak to someone
that this - an automated voice is telling you this call will be recorded, so -
MS HAMMOND: And your own experience, you have said, is that that would discourage
you from proceeding with speaking to somebody?
ADE: Absolutely, I would have hung up. Yes, I would have hung up that first time.
MS HAMMOND: You mentioned that after you spoke to someone from the hotline, you
received a follow-up call. What happened in that call?
ADE: The follow-up - the person I spoke to on the follow-up call certainly was more
helpful, appeared more aware of my concerns, easier to talk to about the concerns. But,
really, at the end of the day, all she could offer was their police intervention program. And
I stated, "Well, surely, if you've got all these - if you have these resources within your
police program, psychologists, counsellors, interventionists, then can I not access them
independently in the community?" But, no, they weren't able to give me any community
contacts at all and kind of call back if I changed my mind.
MS HAMMOND: What are some of the reasons you have felt very reluctant to engage
with a police intervention program or the prospect of your young relative being referred for
engagement with a police intervention program?
ADE: Look, that's just escalating it to a point which is not - would not be helpful right
now. I don't believe we need the police right now. I hope we don't need the police. But to
suggest to a family who are just getting their head around what is actually happening and
what is the significance of happening with their family member to just say, "Oh, your child
has this issue and, hey, let's go to the police", I don't think anyone would want to do that at
all. And that's - look, for me, that's a last port of call.

I hope we don't need it. But I'm glad to know it's there and I'm glad to know it's there for
others, if that's appropriate, absolutely. I'm sure it's 100 per cent useful. I can see they
have quotes online, testimonies how helpful the program has been for people, but that
certainly wouldn't be a first port of call, and I don't think - to think that any family
would - to think that any family would think that's the first place you are going to go, not at
all. No matter what amazing specialists they have or claim to have.
MS HAMMOND: And sitting in a position where you don't feel a police-run program is
appropriate and you feel there would be a lot of reluctance, you have already spoken a little
bit, but what does it seem the alternative, if anything, is?
ADE: Well, there was no alternative offered to me, really. I mean, if you do, you know,
dig through the Step Together website, you know, there is some information on how to
have a conversation with a young person and how to talk about values, if you get that far
with the website. But I know I was wanting somebody locally that we could, you know,
potentially meet with, that they could meet with in person. So that's where, I guess, out of
my frustration, I then reached out to EXIT Australia, who I was aware of through the
media, and also from doing my own search online.
So I just asked them the question, "Hey, do you know anyone in our location who you can
recommend?" And they got back to me and we had, yes, extremely helpful conversation.
Very empathetic and understanding conversation.
MS HAMMOND: So you became aware of EXIT Australia. You chose to contact them.
How were you able to contact EXIT?
ADE: They had an email message form on their website that I was able to email, and then
pretty promptly they got back to me and said, "Would you like to have a conversation?"
So, yes, we arranged a time to speak on the phone and had quite a lengthy conversation.
I felt really comfortable and confident in the person I was speaking with knew what they
were talking about, and that was a great relief, to be speaking with someone who knew
clearly what they were talking about.
When I - my initial question to them was did they know - could they refer me to anyone in
my area, they offered to speak to another psychologist that they worked with in another
state to see if they knew anyone. They got back to EXIT and said they didn't know
anyone. However, the person in the other state was willing to do telehealth and willing to
provide that service. Also I want to say as well, that I had asked other mental health
specialists in the area that I work if they knew anyone working in this area, and they came
back saying no, they knew of nobody.
MS HAMMOND: So you understood EXIT to be a non-government, not-for-profit
organisation who specialises in this space; is that right?
ADE: Correct, yes.

MS HAMMOND: And then they put you in touch with a psychologist, who you were
able to do some telehealth with even though they weren't local. To the extent you feel
comfortable, can you summarise the sort of assistance the psychologist was able to provide
you with in those sessions?
ADE: Sure. Really, it was around - the most valuable assistance was really around family
support, how to communicate and be with family. It was around being able to manage the
moral dilemma because - yes, I didn't - I very - I got to the point where I was - didn't
believe I could hang in there with the young relative. Like, you know, like, you know,
I had other people saying to me, "Oh, well, you know you've got to be mindful of your
own boundaries and take care of yourself."
And as the psychologist and other people, EXIT and other people have shared like "Best
you can to stick with them" and that's bloody challenging. Like, that is really, really
challenging. Like, yes, that's really hard. So really hard.
MS HAMMOND: So they helped you think about not only how you can support your
relative but they also provided support for you -
ADE: Yes, absolutely.
MS HAMMOND: - in a very difficult situation?
ADE: Absolutely and that's what - and even - my intention was, it was like even before,
you know, in the best-case scenario, the young relative would have spoken to that
psychologist. But firstly I would have - it didn't happen. Firstly I would have liked the
young parents to speak, like other family members to have that conversation so that we can
all get on the same page. That would have been my best-case scenario.
It hasn't happened but I'm able to do the best that I can with other family members; not all
family members are coming on board. But yes, I got great - great support and advice
around how to - how to be able to manage that. Yes.
MS HAMMOND: And that's obviously a situation that continues to be real and ongoing
for you at the moment?
ADE: Absolute - yes, it is, absolutely, yes, which is a challenge here speaking about it,
yes.
MS HAMMOND: You've given evidence about how this experience has been difficult to
navigate despite you coming to it with some relevant professional expertise and
experience. Can you share with the Commission some of your concerns about other
individuals who might find themselves in a situation similar to yours and some of the
difficulties you feel they're likely to encounter?
ADE: Well, I think I was able to see the warning signs. Like, I knew what to look out for.
And I think people don't know what they don't know. And so how do family members

know what's happening? I think a lot of the warning signs that Step Together talks about
could be describing any young person or young adult in, you know, too much online
activity and so forth.
But, you know, there's this movement, I perceive it as to be growing. I perceive it as
insidious, and that the - like, the one area when we are talking about young people,
particularly in view of the under 16s not having social media, it's not the social media, it's
the insidiousness of the algorithms that are really targeting them. And that's what we
really need to be talking about. It's targeting young people and also it's targeting adults,
but it is adults as well, not just young people. But I think we need to be cognisant that
people don't know what they don't know and, you know, how do we support others to
recognise those signs.
How do we support others to know that that casual racism and they might joke about it at
home, that normalises an environment where young people can be - you know, it validates
these more extremist views. And, yes, I am concerned with what is happening in the
broader community in regards to the racism that's being enabled to be spoken really freely
and that supports these more extremist views.
MS HAMMOND: At the conclusion of your statement, you say:
"In my view, there's an urgent need for accessible specialist and preventive support for
families and concerned individuals seeking to intervene to help someone they're concerned
about before things escalate."
Is there anything you would like to add to that for the Commission about the real need you
see and the gap you feel you have experienced when trying to access support?
ADE: Yes, the gap in support has been very frustrating, and I could see how a lot of
families wouldn't manage with it. One thing that I've - would have liked would be, you
know, access to timely specialist intervention, but also lived experience support. Like, the
lived experience support from EXIT Australia was really helpful [REDACTED]. Lived
experience peer support really helps, and that's where someone doesn't necessarily need to
have, you know, an academic profession but some training in utilising their lived
experience to support others. I think that could be very powerful in this environment. And
just some meaningful alternatives to the police-led responses.
MS HAMMOND: Commissioner, I didn't have any further questions for this witness.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Thank you, madam. Your evidence is appreciated and you are
excused.
ADE: Thank you.
